questions/x: Here is a vector, x: two across and one up, an arrow on the plane.
questions/one: A dot product asks it one question: how much does x agree with a weight vector, w? Say w is one and one: the answer is three.
questions/more: One answer is rarely enough. Bring two more weight vectors, and the same x gives two more answers.
questions/agree: The second, minus one and two, meets x at a right angle, so its answer is zero. The third, minus one and minus one, points away from x: minus three.
questions/W: Now stack the three weight vectors as the rows of one matrix, W: one row per question. W is three by two.
questions/Wx: Stack the three answers the same way, and they make a new vector: three, zero, minus three. That is W times x, written W x, the two side by side.
questions/turns: So a matrix turns one vector into another. Two numbers go in and three come out, each one how much x agrees with a row.
questions/cayley: In eighteen fifty eight, Arthur Cayley wrote that the idea of a matrix arises naturally from exactly this: a set of equations, each new number a weighted sum of the old ones, written in short: the weights as one grid, beside the list of old numbers.
rows/setup: Now a W with two rows of three, and an x of three entries, one above each column. Three entries take x out of the page, but the recipe never needed the picture.
rows/pair: Entry zero of W x is row zero's answer. Pair row zero with x, entry by entry, and multiply: one times two, two times one, and zero times three.
rows/r0: Add them up: two, plus two, plus zero, is four. That is entry zero.
rows/r1: Row one gives entry one: six, minus one, and six make eleven.
rows/all: So W x is four and eleven. Entry i always comes from row i, both counted from zero.
rows/col: Never from a column. A column of W holds one number per row, two of them here, and x has three: they do not even line up.
shapes/match: Every row is dotted with x, and a dot product pairs entries one to one. So x needs one entry per column of W: three.
shapes/out: And there is one dot product per row, so W x has one entry per row: two. A two by three matrix turns three numbers into two.
shapes/at: In code, the product is W at x, with the at sign of the dot product.
shapes/rule: In shapes: two by three, at three, gives two, the arrow pointing to what comes out. The three of x meets the three columns, and the two rows set the length of the answer.
shapes/big: The sizes can be anything. A ten by three thousand and seventy two W asks an image of three thousand and seventy two numbers ten questions, and turns it into ten numbers.
shapes/fail: Give it an x of the wrong length, and the last column of W has no partner: the product is not defined, and NumPy refuses.
